posts.hook: Your knee pain probably isn't a knee problem.
posts.body:
Your knee pain probably isn't a knee problem.

Stand on one leg for ten seconds. Watch the hip on the side you lifted.

If it drops, or your torso swings out to keep you upright, you found the real issue. The glute on your standing leg has gone quiet, and the pelvis can't stay level without it. The knee pays for that. So does the low back.

I spent years as a physician watching this one leak end people's mobility a decade early. The fix isn't more knee work. It's the hip that stopped doing its job.

One test won't map your whole chain. Ten seconds tells you if you've got a weak link in it.

posts.hook: 'Strengthen your knees' is some of the worst advice in fitness.
posts.body:
'Strengthen your knees' is some of the worst advice in fitness.

Feet shoulder-width, arms straight overhead, squat while you watch your knees in a mirror.

If one or both cave inward, past the line of your big toe, the knee is only doing what it's told. It collapses because the hip above it isn't steering the leg. You can load that knee for a year and it won't hold, because the knee was never the problem.

I see this pattern behind more stalled running and hiking than anything else, and it surfaces in the fifties, right when people blame the calendar.

Train the hip to steer the leg. The cave disappears.

posts.hook: You can't 'sit up straight' your way out of tech neck.
posts.body:
You can't 'sit up straight' your way out of tech neck.

Put your heels, backside, and shoulder blades against a wall. Keep your chin level and touch the back of your head to the wall, without tipping your face up.

Can't reach it? Your head has drifted forward of your spine. Reminding yourself to have good posture won't pull it back, because willpower isn't the thing that's missing. Every inch of forward drift multiplies the load your neck carries all day. That's the stiff neck, and the headaches that follow it.

The head sits forward because the deep muscles that hold it back have switched off. Rebuild those and it comes home on its own.

Good posture isn't discipline. It's capacity you trained or didn't.

posts.hook: One of the best predictors of your independence at 75 is the chair you're sitting in.
posts.body:
One of the best predictors of your independence at 75 is the chair you're sitting in right now.

Stand up from it without your hands. No rocking forward, no push off the thighs.

If you can't, take it seriously. Your glutes and core aren't producing the power to move your own bodyweight, so you've handed the job to momentum. Momentum works until it doesn't, and the day it doesn't is usually the day someone falls.

I watched this on hospital wards for years. The fall was never the start. The start was a chair, a decade earlier, that needed hands.

Rebuild the power to rise while you still have the reserve to build it on.

You don't lose independence to age. You lose it to the strength you stopped training.

posts.hook: Your hamstrings aren't tight. They're stretched, and stretching them more is why they never let go.
posts.body:
Your hamstrings aren't tight. They're stretched, and stretching them more is why they never let go.

Stand sideways to a mirror and look at your belt line. If the front tips down and forward and your low back arches hard, your pelvis is tilted forward.

That tilt anchors the top of your hamstrings and holds them long all day. So they feel tight. And every stretch you do drags on a muscle already at the end of its range. You're pulling on the victim.

The pelvis tips because tight hip flexors haul it down in front while sleepy glutes fail to hold it from behind. Fix that balance and the hamstrings let go without a single hamstring stretch.

Chase the tight muscle and you'll stretch forever. Fix the tilt and it clears in weeks.
